title: Three Hands Clock
context: Grade 5, the pages on the units of time and on reading a clock. An adult sees a clock face with three hands. What the pages are doing is making each hand count its own unit, with the minute hand and the second hand both counting in fives, and making the hour hand move on as the minutes pass instead of sitting on a number.

writeup.why: Name the units of time and how they fit, sort times into a.m. and p.m. by the half of the day they fall in, read the minute hand and the hour hand together, and read a clock to the second with the thin second hand.
writeup.look: One round clock face with three hands, a day bar under it split at noon, and a tally of the turns of the hands.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Three Hands Clock' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of clock readings made. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. One round clock face stands at the left of the area at x 90, y 220, 380 by 380, with twelve numbers and sixty small marks in near-black ink. The hour hand is short and thick and the minute hand is long, both near-black ink, and the thin second hand is longer than both, vermilion, labelled Second hand. Every hand's name is written outside the dial at its rim, so no label line crosses the face. The turning handle stands under the dial at x 200, y 650. The tally stands beside the clock at x 520, y 230, three counters for minutes, hours and days, and each full turn of a hand adds one to the counter of the next. The day bar runs along y 320 from x 520 to x 1110 and is 90 tall: its half from midnight until just before noon stays warm white inside its outline, labelled a.m., its half from noon until just before midnight is rose, labelled p.m., and 12 noon is marked where the halves meet. The time cards wait in a tray at x 520, y 450, each deep blue, labelled Given, and a card lands on the half it is dropped on. On the third phase the number under the minute hand lights amber, and a violet tag beside the dial counts 5 min for each number passed. On the fourth phase a vermilion tag counts 5 s for each number the thin second hand passes, and the reading is built up in green, labelled Answer, at x 520, y 650. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a delete key, and keys for h, min and s. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the nine tools of this chapter share them. What the question gives, as a clock time, a length of time, a start date or a number of days, is deep blue, labelled Given or Start. What the working reaches, as an end time, a length of time, a converted time or a date, is green, labelled Answer, End or How long. The thin second hand and the seconds it counts are vermilion, labelled Second hand. One jump along a time line, and one regrouped unit carried or borrowed, are violet, labelled Jump, Carry or Regroup. On a day bar the half from noon until just before midnight is rose, labelled p.m., and the half from midnight until just before noon stays warm white inside its outline, labelled a.m. The hand, digit, column, jump or date being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open, labelled Place holder, and for nothing else. The hour hand and the minute hand, dials, tick marks, time lines, arrows, operation signs and step labels are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of the content colours, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The clock stays set to the last time read, with its three hands where the child put them and the reading beside it in green.

phases.win: the hour hand has gone twice round and the tally shows 1 day is 24 h
phases.does: turns the thin second hand once round, then the minute hand, then the hour hand twice, and watches the next hand move on each time
phases.goal: 60 s make 1 min, 60 min make 1 h, and 1 day is 24 h
phases.says: Turn the thin hand once round. What has the next hand done?
phases.check: Away from the screen: how many small marks does the minute hand pass in one full turn?
phases.feels: the three hands clicking on together, each turn of one hand moving the next hand one step
phases.hands: Cut a round clock face from card and pin three paper hands to its middle. Turn the thin hand once round while you count aloud, then turn the minute hand once round, and say what the next hand has done each time.
phases.tries: First rung: turn only the thin hand once round and watch the next hand. Second rung: turn the minute hand once round as well. Third rung: the same task with the hour hand and the minute hand only, before the question's own clock returns.

wrong.why: a hundred is the number that groups are usually made of, so it feels natural
wrong.move: writes a hundred for the minutes in an hour
wrong.screen: the answer stays in the slot, the minute hand is turned once round again, and the sixty small marks are counted out in a violet tag beside it

phases.win: the minutes and the hour are read together and turn green, as 35 min past 4

writeup.delight: On the first phase, as the thin second hand finishes its first turn, the minute hand steps on by one small mark, and when the minute hand finishes its turn the hour hand steps on by one number, so the three hands click on together like the wheels of a music box.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet turned. On the first phase one clock face stands with all three hands at the top and a tally beside it for minutes, hours and days. On the second the day bar lies under the clock, its a.m. half warm white and its p.m. half rose, with a tray of time cards beside it. On the third the clock shows a time to set, with the hour hand and the minute hand near-black ink. On the fourth the thin second hand, vermilion and longer than both, is on the clock, and a tray of readings waits below it. One thing moves, once: the turning handle, the first time card, the minute hand or the thin second hand gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: Any time set by turning the hands, any time card dropped on the day bar, and the thin second hand set on any number. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on the units of time, a.m. and p.m., the minute hand and the hour hand, and the thin second hand.
voiceLines: A round clock with three hands, waiting to be turned.
Turn the thin hand once round. What has the next hand done?
Drop the card on the bar. Which half of the day does it land in?
Which number is the long hand on? Count five for every number.
Where is the thin hand? Count five seconds for each number.
A new time on the clock. Read it the same way.
Free play. Turn the hands and drop times on the day bar.
Look at all three hands again. What does each one count?
You turned the three hands together and read a clock to the second.

observations.why: each hand counts one unit, and 60 s make 1 min while 60 min make 1 h.
observations.soWhat: the units of time fit into one another, and the hour hand goes twice round the clock in a day, because 1 day is 24 h.
observations.observe: One turn of the thin second hand moved the minute hand on by a small mark, and one turn of the minute hand moved the hour hand on by a number.

observations.why: a.m. runs from midnight until just before noon, and p.m. from noon until just before midnight.
observations.soWhat: noon and midnight are written 12 noon and 12 midnight, never with a.m. or p.m.
observations.observe: Every card stayed in the half of the day bar it was dropped on, and 12 noon sat where the two halves met.

observations.why: each number the minute hand passes is 5 min, and the hour hand moves on as the minutes pass.
observations.soWhat: read the minutes from the minute hand first, then say the hour the hour hand has just passed.
observations.observe: The hour hand had moved on from its number whenever the minute hand was on a number.

observations.why: the thin second hand goes once round in 1 min, and each number is 5 s.
observations.soWhat: a clock is read as minutes and seconds past the hour, as in 20 min 35 s past 9.
observations.observe: The thin second hand counted in fives too, and its name was written outside the dial.

source_tool.description: One round clock face fills the working area, with twelve numbers and sixty small marks. The hour hand is short and thick and the minute hand is long, both near-black ink, and the thin second hand is longer than both, vermilion, labelled Second hand. Every hand's name is written outside the dial, so no label line crosses the face. A turning handle at the foot of the dial moves the hands together: each full turn of the thin second hand moves the minute hand on by one small mark, each full turn of the minute hand moves the hour hand on by one number, and a tally beside the clock counts the turns up to a day. Under the clock a day bar runs from 12 midnight to 12 midnight. The half from midnight until just before noon stays warm white inside its outline, labelled a.m., and the half from noon until just before midnight is rose, labelled p.m., with 12 noon marked where they meet. A time card, deep blue, labelled Given, is dragged onto the bar and lands in its half. On the third phase the child sets the minute hand on a number and the hour hand follows, moved on from its number for the minutes; the number under the minute hand lights amber and a violet tag counts 5 min for each number passed. On the fourth phase the thin second hand is dragged to a number and counts 5 s for each, and a reading such as 20 min 35 s past 9 is built up in green, labelled Answer. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of clock readings made.
source_tool.art_direction: A round clock on a classroom wall / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: round clock faces with twelve numbers and sixty small marks, a day bar from midnight to midnight, a time line with jumps, columns of hours, minutes and seconds, and month calendars with seven columns.

Every clock time is written in one notation: 4:15 p.m. for a 12-hour time, with a colon and a.m. or p.m., and 1615 hours for a 24-hour time, four digits and the word hours, never a colon and never a dot. Noon is written 12 noon and midnight 12 midnight. A length of time is written 2 h 15 min, 3 days 5 h and 40 s, or in words, and never as a clock time.

Every hour hand sits at its true angle: it moves on from each number as the minutes pass, so at a quarter past it has gone a quarter of the way to the next number. The minute hand is long, the hour hand short and thick, and the second hand thin, longer than both and vermilion. Label lines stay outside the dial.
A time line that passes 12 midnight shows midnight as its own mark and says the next day after it. A count of days always says whether both the first and the last day are counted.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: hands turning, a jump along a time line, a carried unit moving to the next column, or dates being counted on a calendar.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a hand, a digit, a jump or a date the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a time plays in a piece of working: what the question gives, a clock time, a length of time, a start date or a number of days, is deep blue, and what the working reaches, an end time, a length of time, a converted time or a date, is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The thin second hand and the seconds it counts are vermilion. One jump along a time line, and one regrouped unit carried or borrowed, is violet. The half of the day from noon until just before midnight is rose on a day bar, and the half from midnight until just before noon stays warm white inside its outline. The hand, digit, column, jump or date being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open at the front of a 24-hour time. The hour hand and the minute hand are near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Second hand, Jump, Carry, a.m., p.m., Noon and Midnight, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at all three hands again. What does each one count?
voice.onNext: A new time on the clock. Read it the same way.
voice.opening: A round clock with three hands, waiting to be turned.
voice.onFinish: You turned the three hands together and read a clock to the second.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Turn the hands and drop times on the day bar.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has set the hands of a paper clock to times the teacher calls out, and has said what each hand counts. The tool is what turns all three hands together and moves the hour hand on for the minutes, which a paper clock turned one hand at a time cannot show.

answer_key.rule: 60 s make 1 min, 60 min make 1 h, and 1 day is 24 h. a.m. runs from midnight until just before noon, and p.m. from noon until just before midnight. Noon and midnight are written 12 noon and 12 midnight, never with a.m. or p.m. The minute hand moves 5 min from one number to the next, so a minute hand on 7 shows 35 min. The hour hand moves on as the minutes pass, so at 35 min past 4 it is between 4 and 5, past the 4. The thin second hand moves 5 s from one number to the next, so on 9 it shows 45 s. A clock is read as minutes and seconds past the hour, such as 20 min 35 s past 9.
answer_key.wrong: The stage keeps the hands where the child put them. A minute hand set on the wrong number stays, and the number that matches the minutes asked for is lit amber beside it. An hour hand left on its number when the minutes have moved on shows the small step it has yet to take, lit amber. A time card dropped in the wrong half stays there, and the half that holds its time is lit amber. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The hour hand goes once round the clock face in 12 h.
From one 12 midnight to the next it goes round twice.
12 h + 12 h is 24 h, which is 1 day.
items.question: The hour hand goes round the clock face twice from one 12 midnight to the next. How many hours is that, and how many days?
items.checkpoint: 1 day is 24 h, and the hour hand goes round the clock face twice in a day.
items.misconception: Counting one turn of the hour hand as a whole day, when one turn is only half of it.

steps: The p.m. half of the day runs from noon until just before midnight.
The afternoon comes after 12 noon, so it falls in the p.m. half.
Write the hour and the minutes with a colon, then p.m.
So 20 min past 2 in the afternoon is 2:20 p.m.
items.question: Is 20 min past 2 in the afternoon a.m. or p.m.? Write the time.
items.checkpoint: a.m. runs from midnight until just before noon, and p.m. from noon until just before midnight.
items.misconception: Writing a.m. for the afternoon because the day began at 12 midnight.

steps: From one number to the next, the minute hand moves 5 min.
It points to 7, and 7 x 5 = 35, so 35 min have passed.
The hour hand has moved on from the 4 for these minutes, but it is not yet at the 5.
So the clock shows 35 min past 4.
items.question: The minute hand points to 7 and the hour hand is just past 4. What time does the clock show?
items.checkpoint: The minute hand moves 5 min from one number to the next, and the hour hand moves on as the minutes pass.
items.misconception: Taking the hour from the number the hour hand looks nearest to, so the time is called past 5 when the hour hand has only moved on from the 4.

steps: The minute hand is on 2, and 2 x 5 = 10, so 10 min have passed.
The thin second hand is on 9, and 9 x 5 = 45, so it shows 45 s.
The hour hand has just passed the 8, so the hour is 8.
So the clock shows 10 min 45 s past 8.
items.question: The minute hand is on 2, the hour hand is just past 8, and the thin second hand is on 9. What does the clock show?
items.checkpoint: The thin second hand moves 5 s from one number to the next, so a reading has minutes and seconds past the hour.
items.misconception: Taking the thin second hand for a second minute hand because both are long, and reading its number as minutes.

items.question: The minute hand goes once round the clock face. How many minutes is that, and how many hours?
Is 20 min past 5 in the morning a.m. or p.m.? Write the time.
The minute hand points to 4. How many minutes past the hour is that?
The thin second hand points to 6. How many seconds is that?
How many times does the hour hand go round the clock face in 1 day?
items.final_answer: Twice, because 1 day is 24 h and one turn of the hour hand is 12 h

items.question: At which time does the a.m. half of the day end and the p.m. half begin? Write it.
items.final_answer: 12 noon. a.m. runs from midnight until just before noon, and p.m. from noon until just before midnight

items.question: The hour hand is halfway between 3 and 4, and the minute hand points to 6. What time is it?
The minute hand is on 9, the thin second hand is on 4, and the hour hand is just past 11. What does the clock show?
items.final_answer: 45 min 20 s past 11, because 9 x 5 = 45 and 4 x 5 = 20

teaching_notes: Turn the hands of a real clock or a paper clock first. Say the second is the smallest unit this chapter uses, because races are timed in hundredths of a second. Keep a.m. and p.m. to their halves of the day: a.m. from midnight until just before noon, p.m. from noon until just before midnight, with noon and midnight written in words. Say the minute hand points to a number and each number is 5 min, and show the hour hand moving on as the minutes pass: at a quarter past it has gone a quarter of the way to the next number, so it is never on a number. Name the second hand by its thin line and its speed, never by its colour alone.
generation_prompt: Build a clock tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. One round clock face with twelve numbers and sixty small marks. The hour hand is short and thick and the minute hand long, both near-black; the thin second hand is longer than both and vermilion, labelled Second hand. Hand names are written outside the dial. A turning handle moves the hands together, and a tally counts the turns. Under the clock a day bar runs from 12 midnight to 12 midnight, its a.m. half warm white inside an outline and its p.m. half rose, with 12 noon marked between; deep blue time cards, labelled Given, drop into a half. The minute hand is set on a number with a violet tag counting 5 min for each number, the hour hand moves on for the minutes, and the thin second hand counts 5 s for each number. The number under the hand being worked is amber, and a reading is built in green, labelled Answer. Pointer events only, no assets, no network.
